Carl Jung. A Swiss psychiatrist and one of the earliest and most original students of Freud, whom he eventually broke with to develop his own analytical psychology. While Freud rooted the unconscious in personal childhood and sexuality, Jung proposed something far vaster: a collective unconscious shared by all of humanity, populated by universal symbols called archetypes like the Hero, the Shadow, the Wise Old Man, the Anima and Animus, and the Self. Jung's ideas were more mystical and spiritual than Freud's mechanistic drive theory. He integrated Eastern philosophy, alchemy, and mythology into psychology. His framework, particularly the introvert and extrovert distinction and the Myers-Briggs personality framework derived from his work, became deeply embedded in popular psychology and continues to shape how people understand themselves.

Born in Switzerland, Jung studied medicine and psychiatry, becoming director of the Burghölzli clinic in Zurich by age thirty. He met Freud in 1907 and became his intellectual heir and closest collaborator. But their relationship ruptured in 1913 over theoretical differences, particularly Jung's rejection of Freud's emphasis on sexual repression and his more mystical orientation. Jung spent much of his career analyzing myths, religions, and symbols across cultures and traveled to Africa and America to study indigenous psychologies firsthand, seeking patterns that transcended Western assumptions.

At the heart of Jung's theory is the collective unconscious. Beneath the personal unconscious lies a deeper stratum of the mind shared by all humans, shaped by millennia of evolutionary and cultural history. Archetypes are universal symbols and character patterns—the Hero, the Wise Old Man, the Shadow, the Anima and Animus, the Self—that recur in myths, religions, and dreams across cultures and history. The Self is the goal of psychological development, integration and wholeness, symbolized by the mandala. The Self is the archetype of meaning and integration. Individuation is the psychological process of becoming fully oneself by integrating the conscious and unconscious aspects of personality, a lifelong journey rather than a destination. Introversion and extroversion are fundamental personality orientations that determine how the psyche turns its energy inward or outward.

Jung's break with Freud was pivotal for psychology itself. It liberated psychology from a purely reductive, drive-based model and opened it to meaning, spirituality, and cross-cultural symbolism. In an era of increasing rationalism and materialism, Jung's willingness to take myth, religion, and the irrational seriously gave psychology a bridge to the humanities and spirituality. Though the collective unconscious cannot be empirically measured the way Freud's theories could, Jung's archetypes have proven remarkably durable in literary analysis, mythology studies, and narrative design. His insistence that the goal of therapy is not symptom removal but integration and growth shaped humanistic psychology and continues to inform modern coaching and self-development. For many, Jung's psychology feels more liberating than Freud's because it posits not just conflict and trauma but growth, meaning, and transcendence.
